docs.title: B. Development and reasoning exercises

docs.text:
Lines in the Cartesian plane A line should not first appear as a formula to be recognised. We already have all the ingredients needed to construct it geometrically: a point tells us where to begin, and a nonzero free vector tells us in which direction motion is allowed. The two bridge operations from Lecture 2 will be used throughout this chapter: \[ [Q-P]\in V \] is the free vector determined by two points, while \[ P\oplus\mathbf v\in\mathcal P \] is the point obtained by applying the free vector \(\mathbf v\) at \(P\) . Thus scalar multiples and sums are formed inside the vector space first, and only then applied to a point by \(\oplus\) . Guiding question. Which points can be reached from one fixed point by moving only in one fixed direction? Data that determine a line A line in the Cartesian plane is determined by one point \(P_0\) on the line and one nonzero direction vector \(\mathbf v\) . Every point of the line is reached by applying a scalar multiple of \(\mathbf v\) at \(P_0\) . Let \[ P_0=(x_0,y_0), \qquad \mathbf v=[v_1,v_2]
eq\mathbf0. \] Every permitted displacement is the free vector \(t\mathbf v\) , so the corresponding point is \[  oxed{P=P_0\oplus t\mathbf v}, \qquad t\in\mathbb R. \] The types are explicit: \[ t\mathbf v\in V, \qquad P_0\oplus t\mathbf v\in\mathcal P. \] Parametric definition \[  oxed{L=\{P_0\oplus t\mathbf v:t\in\mathbb R\}}. \] In coordinates, \[  oxed{x=x_0+tv_1,\qquad y=y_0+tv_2.} \] Generating a line from one point and one direction Move $P_0$ and $P_0\oplus\mathbf v$, then vary $t$ to generate points of the line. ⛶ $t$ = 1 The vector $t\mathbf v$ is formed first. Applying it to $P_0$ by $\oplus$ produces the point $P(t)=P_0\oplus t\mathbf v$. At \(t=0\) we obtain \[ P_0\oplus\mathbf0=P_0. \] Positive and negative values move in the two opposite orientations. Replacing \(\mathbf v\) by a nonzero scalar multiple changes only the parametrisation, not the geometric line. The same line described by a perpendicular direction Choose a nonzero normal vector \(\mathbf n=[a,b]\) perpendicular to \(\mathbf v\) . For a variable point \(P=(x,y)\) , the expression \[ [P-P_0] \] is the free displacement from \(P_0\) to \(P\) . The point \(P\) lies on the line precisely when that displacement is perpendicular to \(\mathbf n\) . From direction to normal form Since both factors are free vectors, \[ \mathbf n\cdot[P-P_0]=0 \] is a scalar equation. In coordinates, \[ [P-P_0]=[x-x_0,\,y-y_0], \] so \[ a(x-x_0)+b(y-y_0)=0, \] and therefore \[  oxed{ax+by=c},\qquad c=ax_0+by_0. \] The general linear equation is not a second definition. It records the same line by requiring the normal component of the displacement \([P-P_0]\) to vanish. One line, three descriptions Move the point and direction vector and compare the parametric, normal and slope descriptions. ⛶ The direction vector $\mathbf v$, the perpendicular normal $\mathbf n$, and the corresponding coordinate equations describe the same geometric line. Slope form as a special coordinate description Eliminating the parameter If \(v_1
eq0\) , then \(t=(x-x_0)/v_1\) . Substitution gives \[ y-y_0= rac{v_2}{v_1}(x-x_0), \qquad  oxed{m= rac{v_2}{v_1}}, \] and therefore \(y=mx+b\) after collecting constants. The quotient \(v_2/v_1\) has a direct geometric meaning. If \(\alpha\) is the oriented angle from the positive \(x\) -axis to the direction vector \(\mathbf v=[v_1,v_2]\) with \(v_1>0\) , then the direction triangle has horizontal leg \(v_1\) and vertical leg \(v_2\) . Hence \[  oxed{ m= rac{v_2}{v_1} = rac{\Delta y}{\Delta x} =	an\alpha. } \] Thus the slope is not merely a coefficient obtained by eliminating \(t\) . It measures the vertical change per unit horizontal change and is the tangent of the inclination angle. The direction triangle and the slope Move the endpoint of $\mathbf v$ and compare its horizontal and vertical components. ⛶ $m=\dfrac{\Delta y}{\Delta x}=\dfrac{v_2}{v_1}=	an\alpha$ The same direction vector forms a right triangle: its horizontal component is $v_1=\Delta x$, its vertical component is $v_2=\Delta y$, and their quotient is the slope. Vertical case If \(v_1=0\) , the line is vertical and is described by \(x=x_0\) . Parametric and normal forms need no exception; only slope notation fails because neither \(v_2/v_1\) nor \(	an\alpha\) is finite. Three forms, three questions Form What it reveals \(P_0\oplus t\mathbf v\) how a permitted vector displacement produces a point of the line \(\mathbf n\cdot[P-P_0]=0\) which point displacements are allowed \(y=mx+b\) how vertical position depends on horizontal position No representation is the line itself. The line is the geometric set identified by all three. What the familiar Cartesian forms let us read Choose the representation adapted to the question The parametric, normal and slope forms are not competing definitions. They expose different information about the same geometric line. Intersections with the coordinate axes Two sets intersect at those points which belong to both sets at the same time. Thus a point belongs to \[ L\cap M \] precisely when it satisfies the defining condition of \(L\) and the defining condition of \(M\) . For the coordinate axes these conditions are especially simple: \[ 	ext{$y$-axis: }x=0, \qquad 	ext{$x$-axis: }y=0. \] Let the line be \[ L:\quad y=mx+b. \] Intersection with the \(y\) -axis A point on the \(y\) -axis has first coordinate equal to zero. We therefore impose both conditions \[ y=mx+b, \qquad x=0. \] Substituting \(x=0\) into the equation of the line gives \[ y=m\cdot0+b=b. \] Hence the line meets the \(y\) -axis at \[  oxed{(0,b)}. \] In set notation, \[  oxed{L\cap\{x=0\}=\{(0,b)\}}. \] Intersection with the \(x\) -axis A point on the \(x\) -axis has second coordinate equal to zero. We therefore impose \[ y=mx+b, \qquad y=0. \] This gives \[ 0=mx+b. \] If \(m
eq0\) , then \[ x=- rac{b}{m}. \] Hence the line meets the \(x\) -axis at \[  oxed{\left(- rac{b}{m},0ight)}. \] In set notation, \[  oxed{L\cap\{y=0\}=\left\{\left(- rac bm,0ight)ight\}}. \] The procedure is always the same: write the defining conditions of both sets and solve them simultaneously. For an axis, one of the coordinates is simply fixed to zero. Example Consider \[ y=- rac12x+3. \] For the \(y\) -axis set \(x=0\) : \[ y=- rac12\cdot0+3=3, \] so the intersection point is \[ (0,3). \] For the \(x\) -axis set \(y=0\) : \[ 0=- rac12x+3, \] hence \(x=6\) , so the second intersection point is \[ (6,0). \] The line through two points Let \[ P=(x_1,y_1),\qquad Q=(x_2,y_2) \] be distinct points. Their ordinary coordinate difference is \[ Q-P=(x_2-x_1,\,y_2-y_1), \] while the corresponding free direction vector is \[  oxed{[Q-P]=[x_2-x_1,\,y_2-y_1]
eq\mathbf0.} \] Starting at \(P\) , scalar multiples of this free vector generate the required line. Unique line through two points \[  oxed{ L=\{P\oplus t[Q-P]:t\in\mathbb R\}. } \] At \(t=0\) the point is \(P\) . At \(t=1\) , \[ P\oplus[Q-P]=Q. \] This handles vertical and nonvertical lines uniformly. Recovering slope notation If \(x_1
eq x_2\) , \[  oxed{m= rac{y_2-y_1}{x_2-x_1}}, \qquad  oxed{y-y_1=m(x-x_1)}. \] If \(x_1=x_2\) , the line is vertical: \[  oxed{x=x_1}. \] Parallel lines in slope notation Why equal slopes mean equal directions The lines \(y=m_1x+b_1\) and \(y=m_2x+b_2\) have free direction vectors \([1,m_1]\) and \([1,m_2]\) . These are parallel exactly when \(m_1=m_2\) . Parallel nonvertical lines \[  oxed{L_1\parallel L_2\iff m_1=m_2	ext{ and }b_1
eq b_2.} \] If also \(b_1=b_2\) , the equations describe the same line. Slope formulas are efficient consequences of the vector construction, but the parametric and normal descriptions are more general and extend directly to space. Vector tests behind the slope rules Direction-vector criteria \[  oxed{\mathbf v_1\parallel\mathbf v_2\iff \mathbf v_2=\lambda\mathbf v_1	ext{ for some }\lambda
eq0}, \] \[  oxed{\mathbf v_1\perp\mathbf v_2\iff \mathbf v_1\cdot\mathbf v_2=0}. \] These criteria include vertical directions without a special convention. For nonvertical lines take \(\mathbf v_1=[1,m_1]\) and \(\mathbf v_2=[1,m_2]\) . Recovering the familiar slope rule \[ \mathbf v_1\cdot\mathbf v_2=1+m_1m_2, \] so \[  oxed{L_1\perp L_2\iff m_1m_2=-1}. \] This is the slope form of the dot-product criterion, not an independent rule. The nearest point on a line Let \[ L=\{P_0\oplus t\mathbf v:t\in\mathbb R\}, \qquad \mathbf v
eq\mathbf0, \] and let \(P\) be any point. The square-bracketed difference \[ [P-P_0] \] is the free displacement from \(P_0\) to \(P\) . Projecting onto the allowed direction Decompose \([P-P_0]\) into a component parallel to \(\mathbf v\) and a perpendicular component: \[ \operatorname{proj}_{\mathbf v}[P-P_0] = rac{[P-P_0]\cdot\mathbf v}{\mathbf v\cdot\mathbf v}\,\mathbf v. \] The projection is a free vector. Applying it at \(P_0\) reaches the foot \(Q\) : \[  oxed{ Q=P_0\oplus\operatorname{proj}_{\mathbf v}[P-P_0]. } \] Nearest point and distance to a line Move $P$, $P_0$, and the line direction. ⛶ The free remainder $[P-Q]$ is perpendicular to the permitted direction of the line. The perpendicular remainder is \[ [P-P_0]-\operatorname{proj}_{\mathbf v}[P-P_0]. \] Distance in parametric form \[  oxed{ d(P,L) =\left\|[P-P_0]-\operatorname{proj}_{\mathbf v}[P-P_0]ight\|. } \] Every other route from \(P\) to the line contains the same perpendicular component plus an additional component along the line. The perpendicular component alone is shortest. Distance from the normal equation Suppose \(L:ax+by=c\) with normal \(\mathbf n=[a,b]\) . Let \(P=(x_P,y_P)\) and let \(P_0=(x_0,y_0)\) be any point on the line. Reading the normal component The displacement from \(P_0\) to \(P\) is \[ [P-P_0]=[x_P-x_0,\,y_P-y_0]. \] Therefore \[  egin{aligned} \mathbf n\cdot[P-P_0] &=a(x_P-x_0)+b(y_P-y_0)\ &=ax_P+by_P-c. \end{aligned} \] The signed scalar component along the unit normal is \[  rac{ax_P+by_P-c}{\sqrt{a^2+b^2}}. \] Distance is its absolute value. Point-to-line distance \[  oxed{d(P,L)= rac{|ax_P+by_P-c|}{\sqrt{a^2+b^2}}}. \] The numerator measures signed displacement in the normal direction; the denominator normalises the normal vector. Planes in three-dimensional space The point--vector operations introduced in the plane extend componentwise to three-dimensional coordinates. For \[ P=(p_1,p_2,p_3),\qquad \mathbf w=[w_1,w_2,w_3], \] we use \[ P\oplus\mathbf w=(p_1+w_1,\,p_2+w_2,\,p_3+w_3), \] and for two points \(P,Q\) the square-bracketed difference \([Q-P]\) is the corresponding free vector in space. A line was produced by allowing one real parameter, \[ P=P_0\oplus t\mathbf v. \] Only one independent direction of motion was available. Guiding question. What set is obtained when motion from one fixed point is allowed in two independent directions? Let \(P_0\in\mathcal P\) be a point in three-dimensional space and let \(\mathbf u,\mathbf v\in V\) be nonparallel free vectors. Generating the plane Every permitted displacement is a linear combination \[ s\mathbf u+t\mathbf v\in V. \] Applying that free vector at \(P_0\) gives the point \[  oxed{ P=P_0\oplus(s\mathbf u+t\mathbf v). } \] One parameter produces a line; two independent parameters produce a plane. If the directions were parallel, every combination would still lie along one direction. Parametric plane \[  oxed{ \Pi=\{P_0\oplus(s\mathbf u+t\mathbf v):s,t\in\mathbb R\}. } \] If \(P_0=(x_0,y_0,z_0)\) , \(\mathbf u=[u_1,u_2,u_3]\) , and \(\mathbf v=[v_1,v_2,v_3]\) , then \[  oxed{  egin{cases} x=x_0+su_1+tv_1,\ y=y_0+su_2+tv_2,\ z=z_0+su_3+tv_3. \end{cases}} \] Two independent directions generate a plane Change the two vector coefficients and rotate the scene. ⛶ $s$ = 1 $t$ = 1 The combination $s\mathbf u+t\mathbf v$ is a free displacement. The point $P_0\oplus(s\mathbf u+t\mathbf v)$ is obtained by applying that displacement at $P_0$. A normal vector from two directions The plane is generated by two free directions. To write one scalar equation for it, we need a free vector perpendicular to both. In three-dimensional space the cross product is an additional vector operation: \[ V	imes V\longrightarrow V, \qquad (\mathbf u,\mathbf v)\longmapsto\mathbf u	imes\mathbf v. \] Cross product For \(\mathbf u=[u_1,u_2,u_3]\) and \(\mathbf v=[v_1,v_2,v_3]\) , \[  oxed{\mathbf u	imes\mathbf v=[u_2v_3-u_3v_2,\;u_3v_1-u_1v_3,\;u_1v_2-u_2v_1]}. \] Direct substitution gives \[ (\mathbf u	imes\mathbf v)\cdot\mathbf u=0, \qquad (\mathbf u	imes\mathbf v)\cdot\mathbf v=0. \] Thus \(\mathbf u	imes\mathbf v\) is perpendicular to both generating directions and may be used as a normal. Reversing the order reverses the normal, \[ \mathbf v	imes\mathbf u=-(\mathbf u	imes\mathbf v), \] but both normals describe the same plane. From the normal direction to an equation Let \[ \mathbf n=\mathbf u	imes\mathbf v. \] A variable point \(P\) belongs to the plane through \(P_0\) precisely when the free displacement \[ [P-P_0] \] lies in the span of \(\mathbf u\) and \(\mathbf v\) . Since \(\mathbf n\) is perpendicular to both generating directions, \[  oxed{\mathbf n\cdot[P-P_0]=0}. \] Both factors of the dot product are free vectors, so the left-hand side is a real number. For \(P=(x,y,z)\) , \(P_0=(x_0,y_0,z_0)\) , and \(\mathbf n=[a,b,c]\) , \[ [P-P_0]=[x-x_0,\,y-y_0,\,z-z_0], \] hence \[ a(x-x_0)+b(y-y_0)+c(z-z_0)=0, \] or \[  oxed{ax+by+cz=d}. \] Two descriptions, one plane \[  oxed{P=P_0\oplus(s\mathbf u+t\mathbf v)}, \qquad  oxed{\mathbf n\cdot[P-P_0]=0\iff ax+by+cz=d}. \] The parametric equation first forms an allowed free displacement and applies it to \(P_0\) . The normal equation requires the forbidden normal component of \([P-P_0]\) to vanish. A plane through three points Extracting two independent directions Let \(P,Q,R\) be three noncollinear points. Their ordinary coordinate differences are points, while the corresponding free direction vectors are \[ \mathbf u=[Q-P], \qquad \mathbf v=[R-P]. \] Noncollinearity means that these two free vectors are nonparallel. Their cross product \[ \mathbf n=[Q-P]	imes[R-P] \] is nonzero and perpendicular to the plane. Unique plane through three noncollinear points \[  oxed{ \Pi= \left\{ P\oplus igl(s[Q-P]+t[R-P] igr):s,t\in\mathbb R ight\}. } \] \[  oxed{\mathbf n=[Q-P]	imes[R-P].} \] The two expressions have the correct types: the quantity inside the parentheses is a free vector, and applying it at \(P\) produces a point of the plane. Example For \[ P=(1,0,0),\qquad Q=(0,1,0),\qquad R=(0,0,1), \] the ordinary point differences are \[ Q-P=(-1,1,0), \qquad R-P=(-1,0,1), \] and the corresponding free vectors are \[ [Q-P]=[-1,1,0], \qquad [R-P]=[-1,0,1]. \] Therefore \[ [Q-P]	imes[R-P]=[1,1,1]. \] Let \(X=(x,y,z)\) be a variable point. Since \[ [X-P]=[x-1,\,y,\,z], \] the normal equation is \[ [1,1,1]\cdot[X-P]=0, \] so \[  oxed{x+y+z=1}. \] Noncollinearity is essential. If \(P,Q,R\) are collinear, then \([Q-P]\) and \([R-P]\) are parallel and their cross product is zero, so they do not supply two independent directions. Relative positions of planes Let \(P_1\) and \(P_2\) be fixed points on two planes and let \(\mathbf n_1,\mathbf n_2\) be their nonzero normal vectors. Write \[ \Pi_1=\{P:\mathbf n_1\cdot[P-P_1]=0\}, \qquad \Pi_2=\{P:\mathbf n_2\cdot[P-P_2]=0\}. \] Here \([P-P_i]\) is a free displacement and each dot product is a real number. Normals control relative position If the normals are parallel, the planes have the same orientation and are either identical or distinct and parallel. If the normals are not parallel, the planes intersect in a line. Angle and intersection direction \[  oxed{\Pi_1\perp\Pi_2\iff\mathbf n_1\cdot\mathbf n_2=0}, \] and, when the planes are nonparallel, \[  oxed{\mathbf v=\mathbf n_1	imes\mathbf n_2} \] is a free direction vector of their intersection line. The cross product gives the direction because the intersection line must be perpendicular to both normals. A point \(P_0\) on the line is found by solving both scalar plane equations simultaneously. The intersection line is then \[  oxed{ L=\{P_0\oplus t(\mathbf n_1	imes\mathbf n_2):t\in\mathbb R\}. } \] Normals determine how planes meet Compare the three spatial configurations and drag the scene to rotate it. ⛶ Intersecting Parallel Perpendicular The planes, their normal vectors, and the intersection line are displayed in a rotatable three-dimensional scene. Distance from a point to a plane Distance as a normal projection Let \(P_0\) lie on the plane and let \(P\) be any point. The free displacement from \(P_0\) to \(P\) is \([P-P_0]\) . Its scalar component in the normal direction is \[  rac{\mathbf n\cdot[P-P_0]}{\|\mathbf n\|}. \] Therefore \[  oxed{ d(P,\Pi)= rac{|\mathbf n\cdot[P-P_0]|}{\|\mathbf n\|}. } \] Point-to-plane distance For \(ax+by+cz=d\) and \(P=(x_P,y_P,z_P)\) , \[  oxed{d(P,\Pi)= rac{|ax_P+by_P+cz_P-d|}{\sqrt{a^2+b^2+c^2}}}. \] The numerator is signed normal displacement; the denominator converts the chosen normal to unit length. Line and plane from permitted directions A line is generated by one independent free direction, \[ P=P_0\oplus t\mathbf v, \] whereas a plane is generated by two, \[ P=P_0\oplus(s\mathbf u+t\mathbf v). \] The cross product produces a normal, and the dot product turns perpendicularity into the scalar equation \[ \mathbf n\cdot[P-P_0]=0. \] Computational interlude: lines and planes as constructed objects The planar classes Point , AnchoredVector , and FreeVector are those defined in Lecture 2. A line direction is therefore obtained from an ordered pair of points or from another already constructed free vector. The three-dimensional model repeats the same construction in space. docs.title: Lecture 03 · Lines and Planes

docs.text: A line should not first appear as a formula to be recognised. We already have all the ingredients needed to construct it geometrically: a point tells us where to begin, and a nonzero free vector tells us in which direction motion is allowed. The two bridge operations from Lecture 2 will be used throughout this chapter: \[ [Q-P]\in V \] is the free vector determined by two points, while \[ P\oplus\mathbf v\in\mathcal P \] is the point obtained by applying the free vector \(\mathbf v\) at \(P\) . Thus scalar multiples and sums are formed inside the vector space first, and only then applied to a point by \(\oplus\) . Guiding question. Which points can be reached from one fixed point by moving only in one fixed direction? Data that determine a line A line in the Cartesian plane is determined by one point \(P_0\) on the line and one nonzero direction vector \(\mathbf v\) . Every point of the line is reached by applying a scalar multiple of \(\mathbf v\) at \(P_0\) . Let \[ P_0=(x_0,y_0), \qquad \mathbf v=[v_1,v_2]\neq\mathbf0. \] Every permitted displacement is the free vector \(t\mathbf v\) , so the corresponding point is \[ \boxed{P=P_0\oplus t\mathbf v}, \qquad t\in\mathbb R. \] The types are explicit: \[ t\mathbf v\in V, \qquad P_0\oplus t\mathbf v\in\mathcal P. \] Parametric definition \[ \boxed{L=\{P_0\oplus t\mathbf v:t\in\mathbb R\}}. \] In coordinates, \[ \boxed{x=x_0+tv_1,\qquad y=y_0+tv_2.} \] Generating a line from one point and one direction Move $P_0$ and $P_0\oplus\mathbf v$, then vary $t$ to generate points of the line. ⛶ $t$ = 1 The vector $t\mathbf v$ is formed first. Applying it to $P_0$ by $\oplus$ produces the point $P(t)=P_0\oplus t\mathbf v$. At \(t=0\) we obtain \[ P_0\oplus\mathbf0=P_0. \] Positive and negative values move in the two opposite orientations. Replacing \(\mathbf v\) by a nonzero scalar multiple changes only the parametrisation, not the geometric line.
docs.title: Lines in the Cartesian plane

docs.text: Choose a nonzero normal vector \(\mathbf n=[a,b]\) perpendicular to \(\mathbf v\) . For a variable point \(P=(x,y)\) , the expression \[ [P-P_0] \] is the free displacement from \(P_0\) to \(P\) . The point \(P\) lies on the line precisely when that displacement is perpendicular to \(\mathbf n\) . From direction to normal form Since both factors are free vectors, \[ \mathbf n\cdot[P-P_0]=0 \] is a scalar equation. In coordinates, \[ [P-P_0]=[x-x_0,\,y-y_0], \] so \[ a(x-x_0)+b(y-y_0)=0, \] and therefore \[ \boxed{ax+by=c},\qquad c=ax_0+by_0. \] The general linear equation is not a second definition. It records the same line by requiring the normal component of the displacement \([P-P_0]\) to vanish. One line, three descriptions Move the point and direction vector and compare the parametric, normal and slope descriptions. ⛶ The direction vector $\mathbf v$, the perpendicular normal $\mathbf n$, and the corresponding coordinate equations describe the same geometric line.
docs.title: The same line described by a perpendicular direction

docs.text: Eliminating the parameter If \(v_1\neq0\) , then \(t=(x-x_0)/v_1\) . Substitution gives \[ y-y_0=\frac{v_2}{v_1}(x-x_0), \qquad \boxed{m=\frac{v_2}{v_1}}, \] and therefore \(y=mx+b\) after collecting constants. The quotient \(v_2/v_1\) has a direct geometric meaning. If \(\alpha\) is the oriented angle from the positive \(x\) -axis to the direction vector \(\mathbf v=[v_1,v_2]\) with \(v_1>0\) , then the direction triangle has horizontal leg \(v_1\) and vertical leg \(v_2\) . Hence \[ \boxed{ m=\frac{v_2}{v_1} =\frac{\Delta y}{\Delta x} =\tan\alpha. } \] Thus the slope is not merely a coefficient obtained by eliminating \(t\) . It measures the vertical change per unit horizontal change and is the tangent of the inclination angle. The direction triangle and the slope Move the endpoint of $\mathbf v$ and compare its horizontal and vertical components. ⛶ $m=\dfrac{\Delta y}{\Delta x}=\dfrac{v_2}{v_1}=\tan\alpha$ The same direction vector forms a right triangle: its horizontal component is $v_1=\Delta x$, its vertical component is $v_2=\Delta y$, and their quotient is the slope. Vertical case If \(v_1=0\) , the line is vertical and is described by \(x=x_0\) . Parametric and normal forms need no exception; only slope notation fails because neither \(v_2/v_1\) nor \(\tan\alpha\) is finite. Three forms, three questions Form What it reveals \(P_0\oplus t\mathbf v\) how a permitted vector displacement produces a point of the line \(\mathbf n\cdot[P-P_0]=0\) which point displacements are allowed \(y=mx+b\) how vertical position depends on horizontal position No representation is the line itself. The line is the geometric set identified by all three.
docs.title: Slope form as a special coordinate description

docs.text: Choose the representation adapted to the question The parametric, normal and slope forms are not competing definitions. They expose different information about the same geometric line.
docs.title: What the familiar Cartesian forms let us read

docs.text: Two sets intersect at those points which belong to both sets at the same time. Thus a point belongs to \[ L\cap M \] precisely when it satisfies the defining condition of \(L\) and the defining condition of \(M\) . For the coordinate axes these conditions are especially simple: \[ \text{$y$-axis: }x=0, \qquad \text{$x$-axis: }y=0. \] Let the line be \[ L:\quad y=mx+b. \] Intersection with the \(y\) -axis A point on the \(y\) -axis has first coordinate equal to zero. We therefore impose both conditions \[ y=mx+b, \qquad x=0. \] Substituting \(x=0\) into the equation of the line gives \[ y=m\cdot0+b=b. \] Hence the line meets the \(y\) -axis at \[ \boxed{(0,b)}. \] In set notation, \[ \boxed{L\cap\{x=0\}=\{(0,b)\}}. \] Intersection with the \(x\) -axis A point on the \(x\) -axis has second coordinate equal to zero. We therefore impose \[ y=mx+b, \qquad y=0. \] This gives \[ 0=mx+b. \] If \(m\neq0\) , then \[ x=-\frac{b}{m}. \] Hence the line meets the \(x\) -axis at \[ \boxed{\left(-\frac{b}{m},0\right)}. \] In set notation, \[ \boxed{L\cap\{y=0\}=\left\{\left(-\frac bm,0\right)\right\}}. \] The procedure is always the same: write the defining conditions of both sets and solve them simultaneously. For an axis, one of the coordinates is simply fixed to zero. Example Consider \[ y=-\frac12x+3. \] For the \(y\) -axis set \(x=0\) : \[ y=-\frac12\cdot0+3=3, \] so the intersection point is \[ (0,3). \] For the \(x\) -axis set \(y=0\) : \[ 0=-\frac12x+3, \] hence \(x=6\) , so the second intersection point is \[ (6,0). \]
docs.title: Intersections with the coordinate axes

docs.text: Let \[ P=(x_1,y_1),\qquad Q=(x_2,y_2) \] be distinct points. Their ordinary coordinate difference is \[ Q-P=(x_2-x_1,\,y_2-y_1), \] while the corresponding free direction vector is \[ \boxed{[Q-P]=[x_2-x_1,\,y_2-y_1]\neq\mathbf0.} \] Starting at \(P\) , scalar multiples of this free vector generate the required line. Unique line through two points \[ \boxed{ L=\{P\oplus t[Q-P]:t\in\mathbb R\}. } \] At \(t=0\) the point is \(P\) . At \(t=1\) , \[ P\oplus[Q-P]=Q. \] This handles vertical and nonvertical lines uniformly. Recovering slope notation If \(x_1\neq x_2\) , \[ \boxed{m=\frac{y_2-y_1}{x_2-x_1}}, \qquad \boxed{y-y_1=m(x-x_1)}. \] If \(x_1=x_2\) , the line is vertical: \[ \boxed{x=x_1}. \]
docs.title: The line through two points

docs.text: Why equal slopes mean equal directions The lines \(y=m_1x+b_1\) and \(y=m_2x+b_2\) have free direction vectors \([1,m_1]\) and \([1,m_2]\) . These are parallel exactly when \(m_1=m_2\) . Parallel nonvertical lines \[ \boxed{L_1\parallel L_2\iff m_1=m_2\text{ and }b_1\neq b_2.} \] If also \(b_1=b_2\) , the equations describe the same line. Slope formulas are efficient consequences of the vector construction, but the parametric and normal descriptions are more general and extend directly to space.
docs.title: Parallel lines in slope notation

docs.text: Direction-vector criteria \[ \boxed{\mathbf v_1\parallel\mathbf v_2\iff \mathbf v_2=\lambda\mathbf v_1\text{ for some }\lambda\neq0}, \] \[ \boxed{\mathbf v_1\perp\mathbf v_2\iff \mathbf v_1\cdot\mathbf v_2=0}. \] These criteria include vertical directions without a special convention. For nonvertical lines take \(\mathbf v_1=[1,m_1]\) and \(\mathbf v_2=[1,m_2]\) . Recovering the familiar slope rule \[ \mathbf v_1\cdot\mathbf v_2=1+m_1m_2, \] so \[ \boxed{L_1\perp L_2\iff m_1m_2=-1}. \] This is the slope form of the dot-product criterion, not an independent rule.
docs.title: Vector tests behind the slope rules

docs.text: Let \[ L=\{P_0\oplus t\mathbf v:t\in\mathbb R\}, \qquad \mathbf v\neq\mathbf0, \] and let \(P\) be any point. The square-bracketed difference \[ [P-P_0] \] is the free displacement from \(P_0\) to \(P\) . Projecting onto the allowed direction Decompose \([P-P_0]\) into a component parallel to \(\mathbf v\) and a perpendicular component: \[ \operatorname{proj}_{\mathbf v}[P-P_0] =\frac{[P-P_0]\cdot\mathbf v}{\mathbf v\cdot\mathbf v}\,\mathbf v. \] The projection is a free vector. Applying it at \(P_0\) reaches the foot \(Q\) : \[ \boxed{ Q=P_0\oplus\operatorname{proj}_{\mathbf v}[P-P_0]. } \] Nearest point and distance to a line Move $P$, $P_0$, and the line direction. ⛶ The free remainder $[P-Q]$ is perpendicular to the permitted direction of the line. The perpendicular remainder is \[ [P-P_0]-\operatorname{proj}_{\mathbf v}[P-P_0]. \] Distance in parametric form \[ \boxed{ d(P,L) =\left\|[P-P_0]-\operatorname{proj}_{\mathbf v}[P-P_0]\right\|. } \] Every other route from \(P\) to the line contains the same perpendicular component plus an additional component along the line. The perpendicular component alone is shortest.
docs.title: The nearest point on a line

docs.text: Suppose \(L:ax+by=c\) with normal \(\mathbf n=[a,b]\) . Let \(P=(x_P,y_P)\) and let \(P_0=(x_0,y_0)\) be any point on the line. Reading the normal component The displacement from \(P_0\) to \(P\) is \[ [P-P_0]=[x_P-x_0,\,y_P-y_0]. \] Therefore \[ \begin{aligned} \mathbf n\cdot[P-P_0] &=a(x_P-x_0)+b(y_P-y_0)\\ &=ax_P+by_P-c. \end{aligned} \] The signed scalar component along the unit normal is \[ \frac{ax_P+by_P-c}{\sqrt{a^2+b^2}}. \] Distance is its absolute value. Point-to-line distance \[ \boxed{d(P,L)=\frac{|ax_P+by_P-c|}{\sqrt{a^2+b^2}}}. \] The numerator measures signed displacement in the normal direction; the denominator normalises the normal vector.
docs.title: Distance from the normal equation

docs.text: The point--vector operations introduced in the plane extend componentwise to three-dimensional coordinates. For \[ P=(p_1,p_2,p_3),\qquad \mathbf w=[w_1,w_2,w_3], \] we use \[ P\oplus\mathbf w=(p_1+w_1,\,p_2+w_2,\,p_3+w_3), \] and for two points \(P,Q\) the square-bracketed difference \([Q-P]\) is the corresponding free vector in space. A line was produced by allowing one real parameter, \[ P=P_0\oplus t\mathbf v. \] Only one independent direction of motion was available. Guiding question. What set is obtained when motion from one fixed point is allowed in two independent directions? Let \(P_0\in\mathcal P\) be a point in three-dimensional space and let \(\mathbf u,\mathbf v\in V\) be nonparallel free vectors. Generating the plane Every permitted displacement is a linear combination \[ s\mathbf u+t\mathbf v\in V. \] Applying that free vector at \(P_0\) gives the point \[ \boxed{ P=P_0\oplus(s\mathbf u+t\mathbf v). } \] One parameter produces a line; two independent parameters produce a plane. If the directions were parallel, every combination would still lie along one direction. Parametric plane \[ \boxed{ \Pi=\{P_0\oplus(s\mathbf u+t\mathbf v):s,t\in\mathbb R\}. } \] If \(P_0=(x_0,y_0,z_0)\) , \(\mathbf u=[u_1,u_2,u_3]\) , and \(\mathbf v=[v_1,v_2,v_3]\) , then \[ \boxed{ \begin{cases} x=x_0+su_1+tv_1,\\ y=y_0+su_2+tv_2,\\ z=z_0+su_3+tv_3. \end{cases}} \] Two independent directions generate a plane Change the two vector coefficients and rotate the scene. ⛶ $s$ = 1 $t$ = 1 The combination $s\mathbf u+t\mathbf v$ is a free displacement. The point $P_0\oplus(s\mathbf u+t\mathbf v)$ is obtained by applying that displacement at $P_0$.
docs.title: Planes in three-dimensional space

docs.text: The plane is generated by two free directions. To write one scalar equation for it, we need a free vector perpendicular to both. In three-dimensional space the cross product is an additional vector operation: \[ V\times V\longrightarrow V, \qquad (\mathbf u,\mathbf v)\longmapsto\mathbf u\times\mathbf v. \] Cross product For \(\mathbf u=[u_1,u_2,u_3]\) and \(\mathbf v=[v_1,v_2,v_3]\) , \[ \boxed{\mathbf u\times\mathbf v=[u_2v_3-u_3v_2,\;u_3v_1-u_1v_3,\;u_1v_2-u_2v_1]}. \] Direct substitution gives \[ (\mathbf u\times\mathbf v)\cdot\mathbf u=0, \qquad (\mathbf u\times\mathbf v)\cdot\mathbf v=0. \] Thus \(\mathbf u\times\mathbf v\) is perpendicular to both generating directions and may be used as a normal. Reversing the order reverses the normal, \[ \mathbf v\times\mathbf u=-(\mathbf u\times\mathbf v), \] but both normals describe the same plane. From the normal direction to an equation Let \[ \mathbf n=\mathbf u\times\mathbf v. \] A variable point \(P\) belongs to the plane through \(P_0\) precisely when the free displacement \[ [P-P_0] \] lies in the span of \(\mathbf u\) and \(\mathbf v\) . Since \(\mathbf n\) is perpendicular to both generating directions, \[ \boxed{\mathbf n\cdot[P-P_0]=0}. \] Both factors of the dot product are free vectors, so the left-hand side is a real number. For \(P=(x,y,z)\) , \(P_0=(x_0,y_0,z_0)\) , and \(\mathbf n=[a,b,c]\) , \[ [P-P_0]=[x-x_0,\,y-y_0,\,z-z_0], \] hence \[ a(x-x_0)+b(y-y_0)+c(z-z_0)=0, \] or \[ \boxed{ax+by+cz=d}. \] Two descriptions, one plane \[ \boxed{P=P_0\oplus(s\mathbf u+t\mathbf v)}, \qquad \boxed{\mathbf n\cdot[P-P_0]=0\iff ax+by+cz=d}. \] The parametric equation first forms an allowed free displacement and applies it to \(P_0\) . The normal equation requires the forbidden normal component of \([P-P_0]\) to vanish.
docs.title: A normal vector from two directions

docs.text: Extracting two independent directions Let \(P,Q,R\) be three noncollinear points. Their ordinary coordinate differences are points, while the corresponding free direction vectors are \[ \mathbf u=[Q-P], \qquad \mathbf v=[R-P]. \] Noncollinearity means that these two free vectors are nonparallel. Their cross product \[ \mathbf n=[Q-P]\times[R-P] \] is nonzero and perpendicular to the plane. Unique plane through three noncollinear points \[ \boxed{ \Pi= \left\{ P\oplus\bigl(s[Q-P]+t[R-P]\bigr):s,t\in\mathbb R \right\}. } \] \[ \boxed{\mathbf n=[Q-P]\times[R-P].} \] The two expressions have the correct types: the quantity inside the parentheses is a free vector, and applying it at \(P\) produces a point of the plane. Example For \[ P=(1,0,0),\qquad Q=(0,1,0),\qquad R=(0,0,1), \] the ordinary point differences are \[ Q-P=(-1,1,0), \qquad R-P=(-1,0,1), \] and the corresponding free vectors are \[ [Q-P]=[-1,1,0], \qquad [R-P]=[-1,0,1]. \] Therefore \[ [Q-P]\times[R-P]=[1,1,1]. \] Let \(X=(x,y,z)\) be a variable point. Since \[ [X-P]=[x-1,\,y,\,z], \] the normal equation is \[ [1,1,1]\cdot[X-P]=0, \] so \[ \boxed{x+y+z=1}. \] Noncollinearity is essential. If \(P,Q,R\) are collinear, then \([Q-P]\) and \([R-P]\) are parallel and their cross product is zero, so they do not supply two independent directions.
docs.title: A plane through three points

docs.text: Let \(P_1\) and \(P_2\) be fixed points on two planes and let \(\mathbf n_1,\mathbf n_2\) be their nonzero normal vectors. Write \[ \Pi_1=\{P:\mathbf n_1\cdot[P-P_1]=0\}, \qquad \Pi_2=\{P:\mathbf n_2\cdot[P-P_2]=0\}. \] Here \([P-P_i]\) is a free displacement and each dot product is a real number. Normals control relative position If the normals are parallel, the planes have the same orientation and are either identical or distinct and parallel. If the normals are not parallel, the planes intersect in a line. Angle and intersection direction \[ \boxed{\Pi_1\perp\Pi_2\iff\mathbf n_1\cdot\mathbf n_2=0}, \] and, when the planes are nonparallel, \[ \boxed{\mathbf v=\mathbf n_1\times\mathbf n_2} \] is a free direction vector of their intersection line. The cross product gives the direction because the intersection line must be perpendicular to both normals. A point \(P_0\) on the line is found by solving both scalar plane equations simultaneously. The intersection line is then \[ \boxed{ L=\{P_0\oplus t(\mathbf n_1\times\mathbf n_2):t\in\mathbb R\}. } \] Normals determine how planes meet Compare the three spatial configurations and drag the scene to rotate it. ⛶ Intersecting Parallel Perpendicular The planes, their normal vectors, and the intersection line are displayed in a rotatable three-dimensional scene.
docs.title: Relative positions of planes

docs.text: Distance as a normal projection Let \(P_0\) lie on the plane and let \(P\) be any point. The free displacement from \(P_0\) to \(P\) is \([P-P_0]\) . Its scalar component in the normal direction is \[ \frac{\mathbf n\cdot[P-P_0]}{\|\mathbf n\|}. \] Therefore \[ \boxed{ d(P,\Pi)=\frac{|\mathbf n\cdot[P-P_0]|}{\|\mathbf n\|}. } \] Point-to-plane distance For \(ax+by+cz=d\) and \(P=(x_P,y_P,z_P)\) , \[ \boxed{d(P,\Pi)=\frac{|ax_P+by_P+cz_P-d|}{\sqrt{a^2+b^2+c^2}}}. \] The numerator is signed normal displacement; the denominator converts the chosen normal to unit length. Line and plane from permitted directions A line is generated by one independent free direction, \[ P=P_0\oplus t\mathbf v, \] whereas a plane is generated by two, \[ P=P_0\oplus(s\mathbf u+t\mathbf v). \] The cross product produces a normal, and the dot product turns perpendicularity into the scalar equation \[ \mathbf n\cdot[P-P_0]=0. \]
docs.title: Distance from a point to a plane

docs.text: The planar classes Point , AnchoredVector , and FreeVector are those defined in Lecture 2. A line direction is therefore obtained from an ordered pair of points or from another already constructed free vector. The three-dimensional model repeats the same construction in space. docs.title: Computational interlude: lines and planes as constructed objects

docs.text: The companion set contains twenty problems: Problems 01–10 consolidate line generation, equivalent representations, intersections, distance and elementary plane construction; Problems 11–20 require comparison of methods, geometric explanation, spatial visualization and concise mathematical documentation. Open Exercise Set 03 → The line remains the primary object. The final problems extend the same ideas to planes without turning the set into a separate catalogue of spatial formulas.

docs.text: Lecture 03 — Lines and Planes in the Plane and in Space Elementary computational and graphical exercises Write the line through \(P=(2,-1)\) with direction \(\mathbf v=[3,4]\) as \(L=\{P\oplus t\mathbf v:t\in\mathbb R\}\) . Find the points corresponding to \(t=-1,0,2\) and plot them. Find a normal equation \(\mathbf n\cdot[X-P]=0\) and an implicit equation of the line through \(P=(1,3)\) with normal vector \(\mathbf n=[2,-1]\) . Check that \(P\) satisfies the resulting equation. Convert \(2x-3y=6\) to slope-intercept form. Find both axis intercepts and give one free direction vector and one normal vector. Let \(A=(-1,2)\) and \(B=(3,-4)\) . Compute the ordinary difference \(B-A\) and the free vector \([B-A]\) . Write the line as \(\{A\oplus t[B-A]:t\in\mathbb R\}\) and also in implicit and slope-intercept form. Verify both points. Find and plot the intersection of \(L_1:y=2x-1\) and \(L_2:x+y=5\) . Verify the point in both equations. Determine whether each pair is parallel, perpendicular, identical, or neither: (a) \(2x-y=1\) and \(4x-2y=7\) ; (b) \(x+2y=3\) and \(2x-y=4\) ; (c) \(3x+y=5\) and \(6x+2y=10\) . Compute the distance from \(P=(3,1)\) to \(2x-y-4=0\) . Find the foot \(Q\) of the perpendicular and verify that \(d(P,L)=\|[P-Q]\|\) . Write the plane through \(P=(1,2,0)\) with directions \(\mathbf u=[1,0,1]\) and \(\mathbf v=[0,2,-1]\) as \(\Pi=\{P\oplus(s\mathbf u+t\mathbf v):s,t\in\mathbb R\}\) . Produce four points of the plane. For the preceding plane, compute \(\mathbf n=\mathbf u\times\mathbf v\) and derive the normal equation \(\mathbf n\cdot[X-P]=0\) . Verify the four points. Find the plane through \(P=(1,0,0)\) , \(Q=(0,1,0)\) , and \(R=(0,0,1)\) . Use the free vectors \([Q-P]\) and \([R-P]\) to give parametric and normal forms and compute the distance from the origin. Development and reasoning exercises Explain why replacing \(\mathbf v\) by \(2\mathbf v\) or \(-\mathbf v\) in \(L=\{P_0\oplus t\mathbf v:t\in\mathbb R\}\) produces the same line although the parameter traverses it differently. Explain why slope-intercept form cannot represent a vertical line without a special case, while parametric and normal forms handle it naturally. Give one vertical line in all applicable forms. Starting with \(\mathbf v=[a,b]\) , construct a normal vector and derive \(\mathbf n\cdot[X-P_0]=0\) for the line through \(P_0=(x_0,y_0)\) . Explain why the parametric and normal descriptions encode the same line. For \(L=\{P_0\oplus t\mathbf v:t\in\mathbb R\}\) and a point \(P\) , derive \(Q=P_0\oplus\operatorname{proj}_{\mathbf v}[P-P_0]\) . Explain why every other point of the line is farther from \(P\) . A student says two lines are perpendicular whenever their direction vectors have zero dot product. Explain why this is sufficient in the plane but requires an intersection condition for geometric lines in space. Compare \(P=P_0\oplus t\mathbf v\) with \(P=P_0\oplus(s\mathbf u+t\mathbf v)\) . Use one concrete line and plane to explain why one direction produces a one-dimensional set and two nonparallel directions a two-dimensional set. Verify in one numerical example that \(\mathbf u\times\mathbf v\) is perpendicular to both plane directions. Explain why reversing the order changes the normal but not the plane. Give three collinear points and three noncollinear points. Explain what happens to \([Q-P]\times[R-P]\) in each case. Determine the relative position of \(\Pi_1:x+y+z=1\) and \(\Pi_2:x-y+z=3\) . Find a free direction vector and one point \(P_0\) of their intersection, then write the intersection line as \(\{P_0\oplus t(\mathbf n_1\times\mathbf n_2):t\in\mathbb R\}\) . Give a strategy for choosing parametric or normal descriptions when constructing from points or directions, testing membership, finding intersections, checking parallelism or perpendicularity, and computing distance. In every formula identify which expressions are points, free vectors, or real numbers.

docs.text: From a line to a parametric curve The preceding lecture generated a line from one point and one fixed direction: \[ P(t)=P_0+tv. \] The vector \(v\) does not change as \(t\) changes. This is exactly why the generated path is a line. A curved path requires a more general rule. Instead of adding multiples of one fixed vector, we let both coordinates depend on one parameter: \[ x=x(t),\qquad y=y(t). \] The number \(t\) selects a point. As \(t\) varies, the selected point moves and its trace forms a curve. The first question What must change in the description when the direction of the path is no longer constant? One parameter generates a path $x(t)=1+2t,\ y(t)=1+t$ $t=0$, point $(1,1)$ ⛶ Fixed direction: line Changing direction: circle The same circle, another parameter parameter $t$ = 0.00 The parameter chooses a point. Changing the formulas changes the path; changing only the speed of the parameter may leave the geometric curve unchanged. For the circle \[ x(t)=3\cos t,\qquad y(t)=3\sin t, \] we calculate only the four transparent values \(t=0,\frac{\pi}{2},\pi,\frac{3\pi}{2}\) . They produce the four axis points of the circle. The comparison with \[ x(t)=3\cos(2t),\qquad y(t)=3\sin(2t) \] shows an important distinction: the geometric set is the same circle, but the parameter runs through it differently. Three levels that must not be confused the curve is the set of points; the parametrization is the rule that selects and orders those points; time is a physical interpretation of the parameter that requires additional assumptions. Continued in the exercise set Students will generate points, compare two parametrizations of the same curve, restrict the parameter interval and verify generated points in a Cartesian equation. The lecture establishes the distinction; the exercises develop the technique. Parameters that move, scale, and reshape a curve The letter appearing in a formula may play two very different roles. A parameter such as \(t\) selects a point on one fixed curve. A parameter such as \(a\) , \(b\) , \(h\) , or \(k\) changes the curve itself. We use one ellipse to read these roles directly: \[ \frac{(x-h)^2}{a^2}+\frac{(y-k)^2}{b^2}=1,\qquad a>0,\quad b>0. \] The equation is not introduced as a pattern to memorize. It is read geometrically: \((h,k)\) determines the centre; \(a\) determines the horizontal scale; \(b\) determines the vertical scale. Read parameters through their geometric effect centre $(0,0)$, horizontal scale $4$, vertical scale $2$ ⛶ $h$ = 0 $k$ = 0 $a$ = 4 $b$ = 2 Before moving a slider, predict whether the centre, width, or height will change. The animation checks the prediction. For example, compare \[ \frac{x^2}{4}+y^2=1 \] with \[ \frac{(x-2)^2}{4}+(y+1)^2=1. \] The second curve has the same horizontal and vertical scales as the first. Only its centre has moved from \((0,0)\) to \((2,-1)\) . Do not turn this into a catalogue The lecture does not derive every standard equation of a circle, ellipse, parabola, and hyperbola. The purpose is to learn how parameters control position, scale, and shape. Repeated recognition and drawing belong to the exercises. Continued in the exercise set Students will read simple Cartesian equations, vary one parameter at a time, produce a sequence of graphs and document the rule “parameter — geometric effect”. General classification of second-degree equations is outside this lecture. A radial description adapted to a distinguished point Cartesian coordinates answer two questions: how far horizontally and how far vertically? When one point is geometrically distinguished, another description is often more natural: choose a direction by an angle \(\theta\) ; travel a distance \(r\) from the distinguished point. The point is then described by \((r,\theta)\) . Direction and distance Move the point to compare $(r,\theta)$ with $(x,y)$. ⛶ Changing coordinates changes the description, not the point. The pole is chosen because the distance from it matters. The right triangle gives \[ x=r\cos\theta,\qquad y=r\sin\theta. \] Conversely, \[ r=\sqrt{x^2+y^2}. \] Only one elementary conversion is performed on the lecture. For \((r,\theta)=(4,\pi/3)\) , \[ x=2,\qquad y=2\sqrt3. \] The essential idea is not the conversion algorithm. It is the operational reading of a radial equation: Choose a direction \(\theta\) , calculate \(r(\theta)\) , and place the point at that distance from the pole. A radial rule draws a curve $r=2R\cos\theta$ ⛶ $\theta$ = 0.8 The rotating ray and the changing radial distance materialize the meaning of $r=f(\theta)$. The example \[ r=2R\cos\theta \] generates a circle that passes through the pole. We do not spend the lecture converting many radial equations to Cartesian form. One conversion is enough to verify that two descriptions can generate the same curve. Why this coordinate system appears now A focus or a central body is a distinguished point. A radial description records distance from that point directly instead of reconstructing it from horizontal and vertical coordinates. Continued in the exercise set Students will convert several simple points, read radial equations operationally, generate tables of \(r(\theta)\) and compare one radial description with a Cartesian description of the same curve. One parameter organizes a family of conics With the pole placed at a focus, consider the radial family \[ r(\theta)=\frac{p}{1+e\cos\theta},\qquad p>0,\quad e\ge0. \] The parameters have different jobs: \(p\) sets the overall focal scale; \(e\) changes the shape and, at a critical value, the type of conic; \(\theta\) selects one point on the chosen curve. One radial law, four geometric regimes $r=p/(1+e\cos\theta)$ ⛶ $p$ = 2.4 $e$ = 0.60 $\theta$ = 0 current radius: Move $\theta$ to read the formula as a radial instruction. Then vary $e$ and observe how the entire curve changes. The lecture stops at four qualitative cases: Eccentricity Geometric type \(e=0\) circle \(0<e<1\) ellipse \(e=1\) parabola \(e>1\) hyperbola branch This is not a list of four unrelated formulas. It is one family with a shape parameter. For a transparent numerical reading, fix \(p=2.4\) and \(e=0.6\) . Then \[ r(0)=\frac{2.4}{1.6}=1.5, \] while \[ r(\pi)=\frac{2.4}{0.4}=6. \] The two opposite directions have very different focal distances. This is the geometric effect of eccentricity. The transition at \(e=1\) For \(e<1\) , the denominator stays positive for every direction and the curve closes. At \(e=1\) , it can approach zero in one limiting direction. For \(e>1\) , some directions no longer produce a finite nonnegative radius, and an open hyperbolic branch appears. No general second-degree classification and no lengthy algebraic conversion are needed here. The animation carries the qualitative argument; the two hand calculations show how the formula is read. Continued in the exercise set Students will calculate selected radii, create a four-case comparison table, plot representative curves and explain what changes when \(e\) approaches \(1\) from below and above. Focus, directrix, and the geometric meaning of eccentricity The parameter \(e\) has so far been observed through the changing shape of the radial family. We now give it a geometric meaning. Fix a focus \(F\) and a directrix \(D\) . A point \(P\) belongs to the conic when \[ d(P,F)=e\,d(P,D). \] Equivalently, \[ \frac{d(P,F)}{d(P,D)}=e. \] Both distances change as \(P\) moves, but their ratio remains constant. Eccentricity as a constant distance ratio parabola , measured ratio 1 ⛶ $e$ = 1 $\theta$ = 0.4 The brown segment is the distance to the focus. The green segment is the perpendicular distance to the directrix. Their ratio remains equal to $e$. The parabola gives the most transparent first example. When \(e=1\) , \[ d(P,F)=d(P,D). \] For \(e<1\) , the focal distance is smaller than the corresponding multiple of the directrix distance and the curve is an ellipse. For \(e>1\) , the hyperbolic regime appears. The lecture does not derive separate Cartesian equations for all conics from this condition. It uses the construction to explain why the same parameter \(e\) classifies the shapes seen in the preceding animation. Geometry before algebraic elimination The definition compares two distances. Coordinates are introduced only when we need to calculate or draw the condition. The focus, directrix, and ratio are geometric objects independent of a particular coordinate notation. Continued in the exercise set Students will verify the ratio for selected points, draw the two relevant distances correctly and compare the regimes \(e<1\) , \(e=1\) , and \(e>1\) . A full derivation of the radial equation may appear as a developing exercise, not as the centre of the lecture. A conic as a trajectory is not yet a law of motion Conics occur as possible trajectories in an idealized two-body gravitational model. This statement must be read carefully. There are three different levels of description: Geometric path — the set of points forming a circle, ellipse, parabola, or hyperbola. Motion on the path — a rule that assigns a position to each time. Physical law — assumptions and equations that determine which motions are possible. A curve equation supplies the first level. A parametrization supplies an ordering of points and may be used to display motion, but it becomes a physical time law only after additional justification. The path can be classified before the motion is derived ellipse — bounded geometric path ⛶ Ellipse Parabola Hyperbola display parameter $\theta$ = 0 The slider chooses a point on the path; it is not yet a physical time law. The moving point is an illustration of a parametrized path. Its displayed speed is not presented as the physical speed of an orbiting body. At the qualitative level used in this lecture: Geometric type Interpretation in the idealized model circle or ellipse bounded trajectory parabola limiting case between bounded and unbounded motion hyperbola unbounded passage No energy calculation, Kepler-law derivation, or differential equation is introduced here. Those belong to a mechanics course or to the later synthesis after calculus. A curve is not a theory of gravity The statement “the trajectory is an ellipse” does not by itself specify how fast the body moves, why it follows that path, or which assumptions were used. The mathematical model includes the law and the assumptions, not only the shape. Continued in the exercise set Students will classify paths, separate geometric data from parametrization and physical assumptions, identify idealizations of the two-body model and prepare a short note titled “A trajectory is not a law of motion”. What the first four lectures have built The first block of the course now forms one chain. Geometry supplied points, constructions, distances, and shapes. Coordinates encoded points numerically. Vectors encoded changes and directions. Points and directions generated lines and planes. Parameters generated curved paths and organized families of curves. Those curves became components of mathematical models. Two distinctions from this lecture must remain explicit. Parameter on a curve versus parameter of a family The parameter \(t\) or \(\theta\) may select a point on one curve. A parameter such as \(a\) , \(b\) , or \(e\) may instead change the entire curve. Geometry versus model A geometric trajectory is one object inside a model. It is not the motion law, the force law, or the physical phenomenon itself. The conic family also demonstrates a general method that will recur throughout mathematics: Choose a representation adapted to the question, identify the parameters, and observe which properties change and which remain invariant. Cartesian coordinates are useful when centres, axes, and translations are important. A radial description is useful when one focus or central point is distinguished. Neither coordinate system changes the curve; each exposes different information. Bridge to linear algebra The first block concentrated on describing objects and families of objects. The next question concerns an action performed on the entire space: How can one rule move every point and every vector at once? That question leads to linear transformations and matrices. Optional computational model This section is not part of the essential 90-minute lecture. It shows how the central mathematical idea can be represented by one small computational object instead of separate classes for every conic. One class for the radial conic family from dataclasses import dataclass from math import cos , sin @dataclass ( frozen = True ) class PolarConic : focal_scale : float eccentricity : float orientation : float = 0.0 def __post_init__ ( self ) -> None : if self . focal_scale <= 0 : raise ValueError ( "focal_scale must be positive" ) if self . eccentricity < 0 : raise ValueError ( "eccentricity must be nonnegative" ) @property def conic_type ( self ) -> str : e = self . eccentricity if e == 0 : return "circle" if e < 1 : return "ellipse" if e == 1 : return "parabola" return "hyperbola branch" def radius ( self , theta : float ) -> float | None : denominator = 1 + self . eccentricity * cos ( theta - self . orientation ) if denominator <= 0 : return None return self . focal_scale / denominator def point ( self , theta : float ) -> tuple [ float , float ] | None : r = self . radius ( theta ) if r is None : return None return r * cos ( theta ), r * sin ( theta ) The class mirrors the lecture directly: theta selects a point; focal_scale changes size; eccentricity changes shape and conic type; orientation rotates the description. Checking the interpretation conic = PolarConic ( focal_scale = 2.4 , eccentricity = 0.6 ) print ( conic . conic_type ) # ellipse print ( conic . radius ( 0 )) # 1.5 print ( conic . point ( 0 )) # (1.5, 0.0) A computational task based on this code must include numerical checks. Producing a plot without verifying selected values of \(r(\theta)\) is not sufficient mathematical work. docs.text: Lecture 04 — Conic Sections Through Cartesian and Polar Eyes Computational and graphical exercises For the circle \(x^2+y^2=16\) , write a trigonometric parameterisation and a polar equation centred at the circle centre. Mark the points corresponding to \(0,\pi/2,\pi,3\pi/2\) . For the ellipse \(x^2/25+y^2/9=1\) , find \(a\) , \(b\) , \(c\) , both foci, and the eccentricity. Draw a complete sketch with semiaxes and foci. A parabola has focus \(F=(2,0)\) and directrix \(x=-2\) . Derive its Cartesian equation, find its vertex, and draw the equal-distance construction for one point. For the hyperbola \(x^2/16-y^2/9=1\) , find the vertices, foci, eccentricity, and asymptotes. Draw both branches. Convert \((\sqrt3,1)\) and \((-1,\sqrt3)\) from Cartesian to polar coordinates, and \((4,\pi/6)\) and \((3,\pi)\) from polar to Cartesian coordinates. Plot all four points. Convert \(r=6\cos\theta\) to Cartesian form. Identify the centre and radius and explain why it passes through the pole. For \(r=6/(1+\tfrac12\cos\theta)\) , identify \(p\) and \(e\) , classify the conic, and compute its nearest and farthest focal distances. Classify and sketch \(r=3/(1+0.4\cos\theta)\) , \(r=3/(1+\cos\theta)\) , and \(r=3/(1+1.5\cos\theta)\) . Sketch \(r=4/(1+0.6\cos(\theta-\pi/4))\) . Mark the focus, periapsis direction, nearest point, and farthest point. For \(r=4/(1+2\cos\theta)\) , find the angles at which the denominator vanishes, determine where \(r\ge0\) , and sketch the traced branch with its asymptotic directions. Development and reasoning exercises Draw one point in Cartesian and polar coordinates. Derive \(x=r\cos\theta\) , \(y=r\sin\theta\) , and \(r=\sqrt{x^2+y^2}\) . docs.text: One rule acts on every vector In the previous lectures, vectors described changes, directions and combinations. We now study actions on vectors . An action receives an input vector and produces an output vector: \[ \begin{bmatrix}x\\y\end{bmatrix} \longmapsto \begin{bmatrix}x'\\y'\end{bmatrix}. \] For example, \[ \begin{bmatrix}x\\y\end{bmatrix} \longmapsto \begin{bmatrix}2x\\y\end{bmatrix} \] doubles every horizontal component and leaves every vertical component unchanged. The same rule acts on every point, every arrow and every figure. A matrix represents one consistent action We do not choose a new formula for each point. One matrix supplies one rule, and that rule is applied everywhere in the plane. The general two-dimensional rule used in this lecture is \[ \begin{aligned} x' &= ax+by,\\ y' &= cx+dy. \end{aligned} \] The four coefficients are written compactly as \[ A= \begin{bmatrix} a&b\\ c&d \end{bmatrix}, \qquad A \begin{bmatrix}x\\y\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} ax+by\\ cx+dy \end{bmatrix}. \] The output coordinates are linear combinations of the input coordinates. There are no constant terms such as \(+3\) or \(-1\) . The origin stays fixed For every matrix \(A\) , \[ A\begin{bmatrix}0\\0\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}0\\0\end{bmatrix}. \] A translation is therefore not represented by a \(2\times2\) matrix acting on ordinary plane vectors. Translations will require a different representation later. First reading example Let \[ A= \begin{bmatrix} 2&1\\ 0&1 \end{bmatrix}. \] Then \[ A \begin{bmatrix}3\\2\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 2\cdot3+1\cdot2\\ 0\cdot3+1\cdot2 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}8\\2\end{bmatrix}. \] The arithmetic gives one transformed vector. The geometry asks a larger question: what does the same rule do to the whole plane? The columns show where the basis vectors go Recall the standard basis vectors \[ \mathbf e_1= \begin{bmatrix}1\\0\end{bmatrix}, \qquad \mathbf e_2= \begin{bmatrix}0\\1\end{bmatrix}. \] Apply the matrix \[ A= \begin{bmatrix} a&b\\ c&d \end{bmatrix} \] to each basis vector: \[ A\mathbf e_1 = \begin{bmatrix} a\\c \end{bmatrix}, \qquad A\mathbf e_2 = \begin{bmatrix} b\\d \end{bmatrix}. \] These are exactly the two columns of the matrix. Read a matrix as two destination arrows the first column is the image of \(\mathbf e_1\) ; the second column is the image of \(\mathbf e_2\) . Once these two arrows are known, the action on every other vector is determined. Build the matrix by moving its two columns $A=\begin{bmatrix}2&1\\0&1\end{bmatrix}$ ⛶ Drag the endpoints of $A\mathbf e_1$ and $A\mathbf e_2$. The entire grid and unit square follow those two choices. The columns are not merely stored numbers. They are the two vectors that generate the transformed coordinate grid. The original unit square has vertices \[ \mathbf 0,\quad \mathbf e_1,\quad \mathbf e_2,\quad \mathbf e_1+\mathbf e_2. \] After applying \(A\) , its vertices become \[ \mathbf 0,\quad A\mathbf e_1,\quad A\mathbf e_2,\quad A\mathbf e_1+A\mathbf e_2. \] Therefore a unit square usually becomes a parallelogram. The picture is obtained by the same vector addition already used in Lecture 02. Matrix times vector is a linear combination of columns Every vector can be written in the standard basis: \[ \begin{bmatrix}x\\y\end{bmatrix} = x\mathbf e_1+y\mathbf e_2. \] A linear transformation respects this construction: \[ A(x\mathbf e_1+y\mathbf e_2) = xA\mathbf e_1+yA\mathbf e_2. \] If the columns of \(A\) are \[ \mathbf u= \begin{bmatrix}a\\c\end{bmatrix}, \qquad \mathbf v= \begin{bmatrix}b\\d\end{bmatrix}, \] then \[ A \begin{bmatrix}x\\y\end{bmatrix} = x\mathbf u+y\mathbf v. \] This is the geometric meaning of matrix-vector multiplication. From columns to the coordinate formula \[ \begin{aligned} A \begin{bmatrix}x\\y\end{bmatrix} &= x \begin{bmatrix}a\\c\end{bmatrix} + y \begin{bmatrix}b\\d\end{bmatrix}\\[4pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} ax\\cx \end{bmatrix} + \begin{bmatrix} by\\dy \end{bmatrix}\\[4pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} ax+by\\cx+dy \end{bmatrix}. \end{aligned} \] Worked example Let \[ A= \begin{bmatrix} 2&-1\\ 1&1 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad \mathbf x= \begin{bmatrix}3\\2\end{bmatrix}. \] Read the columns first: \[ A\mathbf e_1= \begin{bmatrix}2\\1\end{bmatrix}, \qquad A\mathbf e_2= \begin{bmatrix}-1\\1\end{bmatrix}. \] Because \(\mathbf x=3\mathbf e_1+2\mathbf e_2\) , \[ A\mathbf x = 3\begin{bmatrix}2\\1\end{bmatrix} + 2\begin{bmatrix}-1\\1\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}4\\5\end{bmatrix}. \] The row calculation and the column calculation are the same operation viewed from two directions: rows compute the two output coordinates; columns explain how the output vector is assembled. Do not multiply by position In a product \(A\mathbf x\) , the vector is written as a column on the right. The dimensions are part of the notation, not decoration. A small gallery of transformations The fastest way to learn elementary matrices is to connect each formula with a visible action. In the figure below, the faint grid is the original plane. The transformed grid and the small house show the result of one matrix. One matrix transforms the grid and every figure on it identity — nothing changes ⛶ Identity Stretch Shear Reflection Rotation $A=\begin{bmatrix}1&0\\0&1\end{bmatrix}$ Watch the basis arrows, grid lines and house together. They are three views of the same action. Identity \[ I= \begin{bmatrix} 1&0\\ 0&1 \end{bmatrix} \] leaves every vector unchanged. Horizontal stretch \[ S= \begin{bmatrix} 2&0\\ 0&1 \end{bmatrix} \] sends \(\mathbf e_1\) to \(2\mathbf e_1\) and keeps \(\mathbf e_2\) fixed. Widths double; heights do not. Shear \[ H= \begin{bmatrix} 1&1\\ 0&1 \end{bmatrix} \] keeps horizontal vectors horizontal but moves the top of a figure sideways. A square becomes a slanted parallelogram. Reflection in the vertical axis \[ R_y= \begin{bmatrix} -1&0\\ 0&1 \end{bmatrix} \] reverses the horizontal direction and keeps the vertical direction. Rotation through \(90^\circ\) counterclockwise \[ Q= \begin{bmatrix} 0&-1\\ 1&0 \end{bmatrix}. \] It sends \[ \mathbf e_1\mapsto\mathbf e_2, \qquad \mathbf e_2\mapsto-\mathbf e_1. \] The matrix is reconstructed directly from these two destination vectors. What happens to lines, grids and shapes? A matrix acts point by point, but the results are organized. Lines through the origin remain lines through the origin A line generated by a vector \(\mathbf v\) has the form \[ \mathbf x(t)=t\mathbf v. \] After applying \(A\) , \[ A\mathbf x(t)=A(t\mathbf v)=t(A\mathbf v). \] The transformed points are generated by the single direction \(A\mathbf v\) . If \(A\mathbf v\ne\mathbf0\) , the result is another line through the origin. If \(A\mathbf v=\mathbf0\) , the whole line collapses to the origin. General lines remain lines or collapse A line \[ \mathbf x(t)=\mathbf p+t\mathbf v \] is transformed into \[ A\mathbf x(t)=A\mathbf p+tA\mathbf v. \] This is again a point plus a direction, unless the direction is sent to zero. Parallel grid lines remain parallel or merge All lines with direction \(\mathbf v\) are transformed using direction \(A\mathbf v\) . They therefore stay parallel when \(A\mathbf v\ne\mathbf0\) . Several distinct lines may merge when the transformation loses a direction. Polygons are transformed by their vertices For a triangle with vertices \(\mathbf p\) , \(\mathbf q\) and \(\mathbf r\) , calculate \[ A\mathbf p,\qquad A\mathbf q,\qquad A\mathbf r \] and join the three output points. Straight edges remain straight because the points of each edge are linear combinations of its endpoints. Transform the structure, not isolated dots A useful drawing should display at least two of the following together: basis vectors; coordinate grid; a simple figure; selected input and output points. Seeing only one transformed point hides the action on the plane. Area scaling is visible but postponed The area of the transformed unit square is the area of the parallelogram generated by the two columns. A signed formula for this area is the determinant, which belongs to Lecture 07. Here we only observe whether the parallelogram expands, shrinks, flips orientation or collapses. Questions deliberately postponed At this point we can read a matrix, apply it to vectors, and interpret the result through the images of the basis vectors, the transformed grid, and transformed figures. Several natural questions now appear: How does a matrix change area? Can two different input vectors produce the same output? When can an action be reversed? These questions are important, but they are not part of this lecture. They require the ideas of determinant and invertibility and belong to Lecture 07 . Before that, Lecture 06 will study what happens when one transformation is followed by another. Matrix multiplication will arise from composing two visible actions. Boundary of Lecture 05 Here we only calculate outputs and describe the visible action. We do not yet classify matrices as invertible or non-invertible, calculate determinants, or analyse loss of information. Build a matrix from a picture To construct a matrix, decide where the two basis vectors should go. Suppose an action is required to satisfy \[ \mathbf e_1\mapsto \begin{bmatrix}3\\1\end{bmatrix}, \qquad \mathbf e_2\mapsto \begin{bmatrix}-1\\2\end{bmatrix}. \] Place these destination vectors as the columns: \[ A= \begin{bmatrix} 3&-1\\ 1&2 \end{bmatrix}. \] No system of equations is needed. The matrix is read directly from the drawing. Design procedure Draw \(\mathbf e_1\) and \(\mathbf e_2\) . Draw their required images. Put the image of \(\mathbf e_1\) in the first column. Put the image of \(\mathbf e_2\) in the second column. Test the matrix on one additional vector. For example, \[ \begin{bmatrix}1\\1\end{bmatrix} = \mathbf e_1+\mathbf e_2, \] so its image must be \[ A \begin{bmatrix}1\\1\end{bmatrix} = A\mathbf e_1+A\mathbf e_2 = \begin{bmatrix}3\\1\end{bmatrix} + \begin{bmatrix}-1\\2\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}2\\3\end{bmatrix}. \] Reading a desired transformation Desired action Image of \(\mathbf e_1\) Image of \(\mathbf e_2\) Matrix double all lengths \(\begin{bmatrix}2\\0\end{bmatrix}\) \(\begin{bmatrix}0\\2\end{bmatrix}\) \(\begin{bmatrix}2&0\\0&2\end{bmatrix}\) reflect in the horizontal axis \(\begin{bmatrix}1\\0\end{bmatrix}\) \(\begin{bmatrix}0\\-1\end{bmatrix}\) \(\begin{bmatrix}1&0\\0&-1\end{bmatrix}\) swap the coordinate axes \(\begin{bmatrix}0\\1\end{bmatrix}\) \(\begin{bmatrix}1\\0\end{bmatrix}\) \(\begin{bmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{bmatrix}\) project onto the vertical axis \(\begin{bmatrix}0\\0\end{bmatrix}\) \(\begin{bmatrix}0\\1\end{bmatrix}\) \(\begin{bmatrix}0&0\\0&1\end{bmatrix}\) The first row is not the first basis image Basis images are stored in columns . Confusing rows with columns usually produces a different transformation, often a reflection or shear in an unintended direction. Quick visual test If the two columns point in exactly the same direction, can the image still fill the plane? Explain using linear combinations of the columns.
